title: TypeScript Generics: From Basics to Type-Level Programming
summary: Study notes on TypeScript generics: generic functions, interfaces and classes, constraints, keyof and indexed access, defaults, inference, conditional and mapped types, built-in utility types, and variance. Ends with common mistakes and a cheatsheet.

chapters.title: Why Generics: Generic Functions
points: Generics are type parameters: types passed in like function arguments, written in angle brackets <T>
Problem: function identity(x: any): any loses the type; the caller gets any back
Fix: function identity<T>(x: T): T links the input type to the output type
Explicit call identity<string>('a') versus inferred call identity('a') where T is inferred as string
Literal inference: identity('a') with const T gives 'a'; a plain T gives string
Multiple type params: function pair<A, B>(a: A, b: B): [A, B]
Arrow generics in .tsx files need <T,> or <T extends unknown> to avoid being parsed as JSX
Generics versus unions: (x: string | number) => string | number does not link in to out; <T extends string | number>(x: T): T does
Generics are erased at compile time, so there is zero runtime cost and T cannot be used as a value
Example: function first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined returns number | undefined for number[]
Example: function map<T, U>(arr: T[], fn: (x: T) => U): U[] infers both T and U from the call
Rule of thumb: if a type parameter appears only once in a signature, it is probably not needed

chapters.title: Generic Interfaces, Type Aliases and Classes
points: Generic interface: interface Box<T> { value: T }; use it as Box<number>
Generic type alias: type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E }
Generic function type: type Mapper<T, U> = (x: T) => U
Interface with a generic method versus a generic interface: the type param belongs to the whole type or to one call
Generic class: class Stack<T> { private items: T[] = []; push(x: T) {...}; pop(): T | undefined {...} }
new Stack<number>() fixes T for the whole instance; new Stack() with no hint falls back to unknown
Static members cannot use the class type parameter, because T belongs to instances
Generic factory: function create<T>(ctor: new () => T): T
Generic React-style example: type Props<T> = { items: T[]; render: (item: T) => string }
Generic constructor inference: new Box(5) infers Box<number>
Type alias versus interface for generics: aliases can express unions and conditionals, interfaces can be merged
Naming conventions: T, U, K, V, E, or descriptive names like TItem when there are several

chapters.title: Constraints with extends
points: T extends X means T must be assignable to X; it is an upper bound, not inheritance
function len<T extends { length: number }>(x: T): T: accepts strings, arrays and objects with a length
Without the constraint, x.length is an error because T could be anything
The constraint keeps the specific type: it returns T, not { length: number }
Constraint with a union: T extends string | number
Constraint referencing another param: <T, K extends keyof T>
Constraint with a constructor: T extends new (...args: any[]) => object (mixins)
Constraint on a generic interface: interface Repo<T extends { id: string }>
Common mistake: T extends object accepts arrays and functions too
Common mistake: returning a plain {} where T is expected fails, because T may be a narrower subtype
Common mistake: confusing T extends U (constraint) with the conditional type T extends U ? A : B
Use T extends unknown as a no-op bound, and {} or NonNullable to exclude null/undefined

chapters.title: keyof, typeof and Indexed Access Types
points: keyof T produces the union of T's known property names: keyof {a: 1, b: 2} is 'a' | 'b'
Indexed access: T[K] is the type of property K on T, such as Person['name']
Classic: function getProp<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]
getProp({a: 1}, 'b') is a compile error because 'b' is not keyof {a: number}
T[keyof T] gives the union of all value types
Array element type: string[][number] is string; also typeof tuple[number]
typeof value in a type position captures a value's type: type Cfg = typeof config
keyof typeof obj gives the union of the object's keys
as const plus typeof gives literal unions: const dirs = ['up','down'] as const; type Dir = (typeof dirs)[number]
keyof on a type with a string index signature gives string | number
keyof any is string | number | symbol
Mistake: keyof returns property keys, not values; use T[keyof T] for values
Mistake: assuming Object.keys(obj) is typed as (keyof T)[]; it returns string[]

chapters.title: Default Type Parameters and Inference
points: Default: interface Response<T = unknown>, so Response alone means Response<unknown>
Defaults must come after required params: <T, U = string> is valid, <T = string, U> is an error
A default can reference earlier params: <T, U = T[]>
A default is not a constraint: <T extends string = 'a'> sets both
Defaults apply when there is no inference candidate and no explicit argument
Inference sources: arguments, return-type context, contextual typing of callbacks
Inference from multiple candidates: f<T>(a: T, b: T) with (1, 'x') errors, or infers a union with a looser signature
Partial explicit args are not allowed: f<string>(...) forces every param to be written or defaulted, with no partial inference
Inference fails when T appears only in the return type: function make<T>(): T gives unknown
Inference fails when T is only in a non-inferrable position, such as a callback return that depends on a hand-written annotation
NoInfer<T> (TS 5.4) blocks a position from contributing candidates: <T>(items: T[], d: NoInfer<T>)
Workaround for partial inference: currying, e.g. make<A>() returning <B>(b: B) => ..., or use satisfies
const type parameters (TS 5.0): <const T>(x: T) infers readonly literals without as const

chapters.title: Conditional Types and infer
points: Syntax: T extends U ? X : Y, resolved at the type level
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false
Distribution: with a naked type parameter, a union is split across members: ToArray<string | number> is string[] | number[]
Block distribution by wrapping: [T] extends [U] ? X : Y
never is the empty union, so a distributive conditional over never yields never
infer declares a type variable inside the extends clause: T extends Array<infer U> ? U : never
Own ReturnType: type RT<F> = F extends (...a: any[]) => infer R ? R : never
Own Awaited-style unwrap: T extends Promise<infer U> ? Unwrap<U> : T (recursive)
Infer multiple positions: T extends (infer A)[] ? A : never; function params via infer P
infer ... extends (TS 4.7): T extends [infer H extends string, ...any[]] narrows H
Template literal inference: S extends `${infer A}-${infer B}` ? [A, B] : never
Mistake: expecting a conditional on a generic body to resolve; it is deferred until T is known
Mistake: boolean is true | false, so IsString<boolean>-style checks distribute and give a union

chapters.title: Mapped Types
points: Syntax: { [K in keyof T]: T[K] } builds a new type by looping over keys
Homomorphic mapped types (K in keyof T) preserve modifiers like readonly and ?
Modifiers: +readonly / -readonly and +? / -? add or remove them; -? makes optional keys required
Transform values: { [K in keyof T]: Promise<T[K]> }
Key remapping with as (TS 4.1): { [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<K & string>}`]: () => T[K] }
Filter keys with as and never: { [K in keyof T as T[K] extends Function ? never : K]: T[K] }
Map over a union of literals: { [K in 'a' | 'b']: number } makes an object type
Mapping over arrays and tuples: a homomorphic map on T[] gives a mapped array
Remove readonly: type Mutable<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }
Deep versions need recursion: type DeepPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> }
Mapped type versus index signature: mapped types need a known key union, index signatures allow any key
Mapped types versus Record: Record<K, V> is the non-homomorphic form with no modifier preservation

chapters.title: Built-in Utility Types
points: Partial<T> makes every property optional: { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }, useful for update payloads
Required<T> removes ? from every property: -?
Readonly<T> adds readonly to every property; it is shallow and compile-time only
Pick<T, K extends keyof T> keeps only the listed keys: Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'>
Omit<T, K extends keyof any> drops keys: Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>; K is not checked against T's keys
Record<K, V> builds an object type from a key union: Record<'a' | 'b', number>
ReturnType<F> extracts a function's return type; Parameters<F> gives the args tuple
Exclude<U, X> removes union members; Extract<U, X> keeps matching members
NonNullable<T> strips null and undefined
Awaited<T> unwraps promises recursively; combine as Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fn>>
Omit on a union does not distribute: Omit<A | B, 'x'> collapses to common keys, so write a distributive version
InstanceType<C> and ConstructorParameters<C> work on class constructors

chapters.title: Variance Basics
points: Variance describes how subtyping of T relates to subtyping of Box<T>
Covariant: Dog extends Animal implies Box<Dog> extends Box<Animal>; fits producers like readonly arrays and return types
Contravariant: Dog extends Animal implies Handler<Animal> extends Handler<Dog>; fits consumers like parameters
Invariant: no assignment either way; fits mutable read/write positions
Function types: parameters are contravariant under strictFunctionTypes, return types are covariant
Method shorthand is bivariant even under strictFunctionTypes: m(x: T) differs from m: (x: T) => void
Arrays are unsoundly covariant in TS: Animal[] = dogs is allowed, then pushing a Cat compiles
Explicit annotations (TS 4.7): interface Producer<out T>, interface Consumer<in T>, and in out T for invariant
Variance annotations are checked against the structure, and they speed up assignability checks
Example: (a: Animal) => void is assignable to (d: Dog) => void, but not the reverse
Rule: out means T only appears in output positions, in means only input positions, and both means invariant
Check with a probe: type Check = Box<Dog> extends Box<Animal> ? 1 : 0

chapters.title: Trade-offs, Pitfalls and Common Mistakes
points: Over-generic code: a function with five type params that nobody can read; prefer simple overloads
Unnecessary generic: function log<T>(x: T): void is the same as (x: unknown) => void
Type-parameter-used-once lint rule: no-unnecessary-type-parameters flags it
Casting inside generics: return {} as T hides a real bug, because the value may not satisfy T
Excessive recursion: 'Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite' appears at about 50 levels, with a tail-recursive limit near 1000
Compile-time cost: heavy conditional and mapped types slow tsc and the editor; measure with --generateTrace
Error messages from deep generics are unreadable; show them with a Simplify<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] } & {} wrapper
Generics versus overloads: overloads give clean per-case signatures, generics with conditionals give one signature but a weaker body check
Generics versus unknown: use unknown for values you only pass around, generics when the output depends on the input
Assuming T is available at runtime: you cannot do new T() or typeof T, so pass a constructor or a tag value
Object.keys, JSON.parse and Object.entries lose generics, so cast at one small boundary
Test types with expectTypeOf or tsd, because type-level code needs tests too

chapters.title: Cheatsheet: TypeScript Generics at a Glance
points: Generic function: function f<T>(x: T): T
Constraint: <T extends { id: string }>
Key lookup: <T, K extends keyof T>(o: T, k: K): T[K]
Default: <T = unknown>
Conditional: T extends U ? X : Y; distributes over unions when T is naked
infer: T extends (...a: any[]) => infer R ? R : never
Mapped: { [K in keyof T]: ... }, with -? and -readonly, and as for remapping
Utility table: Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType, Parameters, Awaited, NonNullable, Exclude, Extract
Variance: out means covariant, in means contravariant, in out means invariant
NoInfer<T> and const T control inference; TS 5.4 and 5.0
Debug trick: wrap a type in Simplify<T>, or hover with a type alias to see expanded shapes
Summary: generics link types, constraints bound them, keyof and indexed access index them, conditional and mapped types transform them
